title: Lab4CE: a Remote Laboratory for Computer Education
extended_summary:
This paper addresses how to improve engagement and learning in remote practical activities for computer science education, with an emphasis on the scaffolding needed around virtual laboratories. The authors argue that virtualization alone is not sufficient for effective learning, and ask how scaffolding, collaboration, awareness, and learning analytics can increase students’ engagement in remote lab work.

To address this problem, they introduce Lab4CE, a remote laboratory for computer education built on a three-layer architecture. The environment includes an experiment authoring tool for instructors, a rich learning interface for students and tutors, instant messaging, artifact-awareness tools showing who is doing what on shared resources, learning analytics timelines, and a management dashboard for tutors. The system supports both individual and collaborative practical sessions over virtual machines and networked resources.

The paper reports an exploratory study with 139 first-year undergraduate computer science students at the University of Toulouse, France, in a face-to-face course on Linux system use. Students could optionally use Lab4CE to practice file, folder, permission, and process management tasks. Results suggest the system had a positive effect on engagement, as many students used the remote lab rather than only practicing on their own computers, and there was a significant positive correlation between activity in the system and achievement on a later academic test. The authors conclude that scaffolding and analytics can support remote computer science practical work, while noting that intelligent tutoring remains a future improvement.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed exploratory correlational study, not an RCT or QED. The evidence is useful but limited by self-selection, missing comparison equivalence, and the fact that the main achievement result is a correlation rather than a causal estimate.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported association between system activity and achievement is moderate in size (r=0.41), which indicates a meaningful positive relationship. However, because the design is observational and the intervention is a broader remote lab environment rather than a tightly controlled treatment, the practical impact is promising but not definitive.

interventions.use_case: remote virtual laboratory for computer science practical work with scaffolding tools, shared control, chat, awareness, analytics, and authoring for Linux/system administration exercises

finding.finding_summary: In an exploratory study with 139 first-year computer science students, the authors report that the Lab4CE remote laboratory appeared to increase engagement in practical learning. Usage data showed that more than 50% of students used a virtual machine in Lab4CE, compared with 25% who installed their own Linux VM, and students opened 477 sessions with a mean duration of 39 minutes.
finding.measure: Engagement / on-task behavior in remote practical activities; system usage logs (sessions, duration, commands)

finding.finding_summary: The study found a significant positive correlation between students’ activity in Lab4CE and their learning achievement on the final test. Using 55 students and 17 test questions after filtering, the authors report Pearson’s r=0.41 (p=.002) between activity level and achievement, suggesting that more active use of the system was associated with better performance.
finding.measure: Final academic achievement test on Linux/system administration topics
